What Is Glass Made Of? So what, exactly, is glass made of? At its heart, glass is silica, the very same silicon dioxide (SiO2) that makes up ordinary sand. Silica on its own can be turned into glass, but it is an expensive way to do it, because pure silica only melts at around 1700 °C (3092 °F). To make the everyday glass in your windows and drinking bottles far more cheaply, manufacturers blend the sand with two other ingredients. The first is soda ash (sodium carbonate, Na2CO3), which lowers the temperature at which the sand melts and makes the batch much easier to work. The second is limestone (calcium carbonate, CaCO3); without it, a glass made from just soda and sand would slowly dissolve in water, and the lime is what makes the finished product tough and durable. The result is called soda-lime-silica glass, and it accounts for the overwhelming majority of the glass produced worldwide, from bottles and jars to flat window panes. As the batch heats up, the carbonates break down: limestone (CaCO3) decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, while soda ash (Na2CO3) reacts with the silica to form sodium silicates, again releasing carbon dioxide gas. New compounds are formed and CO2 bubbles out of the melt, which are both hallmarks of a chemical change. So the tidy classroom answer is this: melting pure sand, or re-melting old glass, into fresh glass is a physical change, whereas cooking up commercial soda-lime glass from scratch is a mix of both, driven by real chemical reactions inside the furnace. Inside the Furnace An industrial glass furnace is a large, continuously operating tank that can hold hundreds of tons of molten glass at once. Raw materials, collectively called “batch,” are fed in at one end and molten glass is drawn out at the other. Furnace temperatures typically sit between about 1,400 °C and 1,600 °C, depending on the glass type. The batch floats on top of the existing melt and gradually dissolves as the carbonates decompose, releasing carbon dioxide.
